Kalshiâs newly introduced American Power Index takes the question every cable segment fights over (who is really winning the contest for power in Washington) and answers it with a single number.

Iâve always been fascinated by solving problems. First, they were math problems in primary school. Then, math, physics, and engineering problems in high school. Then, applying math to decision and control problems in college. Then, applying statistical methods to forecasting problems. Today, Iâve moved on to solving complex tech giant-building problems, but when you break down most complex problems into simpler ones, they often come down to predicting risks and forecasting expected value. Over the years, Iâve learned that the best people, groups of people, algorithms, or systems of algorithms for forecasting the future are full-spectrum signal processors rather than narrow-band signal amplifiers.

Try a small experiment. Ask a dozen random people whether the country is drifting left or right, and youâll get a dozen confident, incompatible answers, most of them shaped by whichever sources that person already trusts. Media outlets are competing for eyeballs. Polling tells you what people are willing to say out loud. Your feed tells you what your particular corner of the internet wants to be true. None is a reliable guide to what actually comes next. We are buried in political information and starved for political clarity.

That gap is widening. We are wired to seek out what confirms the story we already hold. Year after year, the payoff for being loud has outrun the payoff for being right, and weâve sorted ourselves into audiences that rarely see the same facts, let alone agree on them. When it is time for political debates, we have already picked a side, and our natural inclination is to root for our team rather than get to the truth.

Recent findings suggest that one mechanism has been consistently strong as a full-spectrum signal processor rather than a narrow-band signal amplifier: the market. Markets make people back beliefs with capital, and capital has a way of sharpening judgment that pundit commentary never will. Anyone can hold a view for free; holding a financial position costs you if youâre wrong. What comes out the other end is a price: a continuously updated consensus of everyone with money and conviction on the line, stripped of the performance that dominates everywhere else. If you care what is likely to happen rather than what is smart or fashionable to say, the price is the better witness.

According to recent reports, that is the case for what Kalshi introduced: the Kalshi American Power Index, or KPOW. It is an S&P 500 for politics. It compresses a vast, churning system into one number you can track. KPOW runs on a scale from +50 on the Democratic side to +50 on the Republican side, and it blends two layers: a quarter of the weight reflects the certified reality of who controls the House, Senate, and presidency today, while three quarters reflects what Kalshiâs markets imply about who controls them next, assembled from six pieces, ranging from chamber control to expected seat margins to the odds of a government shutdown. The mechanics matter less than what they produce: a single line that moves when power actually shifts, not just when people comment on it.

What we find most compelling isnât where the number sits on a given day; itâs what happens when it moves. A poll is a still photo taken on the afternoon someone happened to ask. An index is a continuous recording. A court ruling, a primary upset, or a shock from overseas indicates up as a bend in the line you can point to and size. That converts vague arguments into something testable. Did the redistricting decision actually move power, or did it just own a news cycle? You used to be able to debate that endlessly. Now thereâs a measurement to debate against.

Sources indicate that prediction markets built their reputation on questions with a finish line: a winner, a vote, a clear settlement. The questions that shape how we feel about the country mostly donât have a single answer. âWhich way is power tilting?â never resolves; it simply keeps shifting. An index is what allows a market to address a question like that, not by crowning a winner, but by returning a number, the way an equity index distills an entire economy into a single readable figure. Kalshi could already price the questions that end. As of today, it can price the ones that donât.

And none of this exists without the exchange underneath it. An index is only as trustworthy as the markets feeding it, which means it requires the kind of liquidity, regulation, and settlement infrastructure that takes years to build. Kalshi has spent those years. And once that foundation exists, an index is just the first instrument it supports. The same layer can carry a whole catalog of contracts tied to questions that the legacy financial system was never designed to touch.

In a recent development, the defining questions of the coming decade, across politics, policy, technology, and markets, will mostly be the messy, never-quite-settled kind, and theyâll arrive buried in more noise than ever. The opportunity is to give people a way to measure those questions rather than just shouting past one another about them. Thatâs why weâre proud to back Tarek, Luana, and the Kalshi team. The contest for power will keep swinging back and forth. For the first time, we can actually watch it move.

Thanksgiving is over, and the Black Friday laptop deals are rolling in. As WIRED’s head laptop reviewer, I’m seeing solid discounts on some of the best laptops I’ve tested this year, whether you’re looking for a upcoming MacBook, Windows laptop, or gaming device.

It has been revealed that want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Black Friday Deals, the Best Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best Tech Deals.

Sources indicate that discounts on already budget-oriented laptops are often sparse. That’s been true for the Dell XPS 13 ever since it relaunched a few months ago, holding steady at a starting price of either $700 or $750. But for Black Friday, Dell’s dropped the price by $200 to just $550. It’s astounding that you can get a laptop of this caliber for that price, especially given how premium it feels. The chassis is well-built and highly portable; the display is both bright and colorful, and the trackpad feels great to use. However, this $550 model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which might be a sticking point for many people. You can upgrade to 16 GB, but it’s not on sale for Black Friday.

Back in June, Apple raised the price of the MacBook Air to $1,299. It felt inevitable, but as a laptop reviewer, it still crushed my spirits. The M5 MacBook Air is the laptop most people should buy, but at $1,299, I knew it was a stretch for most budgets. That’s what makes this Amazon discount feel so impactful. It brings the MacBook Air down to $1,049, making it the first time it’s been close to its original price since June.

The MacBook Neo is already cheap, so Apple has no incentive to cut the price—even though the laptop has been out for seven months. But finally, the MacBook Neo’s price has dropped by $50, bringing it down to $649. That’s a great deal, especially if you’re looking for an affordable laptop that feels premium, with a metal chassis and quality display. The 8 GB of RAM is limiting, but if your needs aren’t overly heavy, the MacBook Neo should do the trick—especially at this price.

Industry observers note that these days, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a laptop under $1,000 without major compromises. That’s even more uncommon for a laptop with a larger screen. But the IdeaPad Slim 5x is just that. It’s a 15-inch laptop with great performance, long-lasting battery life, lots of ports, a solid trackpad, and a high-resolution OLED screen. It even comes packed to the brim with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. It’s not as thin as the 15-inch MacBook Air, but it’s hundreds of dollars cheaper.

Sources indicate that it might be well over two years old, but I still recommend the 2024 Surface Laptop. The price is down to $900 right now, which is a good deal for these specs, performance, and battery life. You’re limited to the blue color option (also known as Sapphire), but it’s the best price I’ve seen on this laptop so far this year. My favorite feature will always be the 3:2 aspect ratio screen, which gives the display a taller shape for more vertical space to work with.

It has been revealed that there is a newer version that uses the Snapdragon X2 Plus/Elite chips, but I find it quite expensive. The IdeaPad Slim 5x listed above is the better option if you’re OK with a larger device, since it uses those next-generation Snapdragon chips and twice the storage. But if you’re sold on the Surface Laptop's more premium design, this is the one to get.

With the MacBook Neo selling for $600, you might look at something like the HP OmniBook 5 with suspicion. Even on sale for $700, being $100 more than the MacBook Neo doesn’t seem like a great position for an entry-level Windows laptop. And while this laptop is often on sale, this is $100 cheaper than I’ve seen it over the past few weeks.

But the HP OmniBook 5 is a special device, with its OLED display, very thin chassis, and 16 GB of RAM. It very much looks like a laptop that should cost hundreds more. Battery life is great, too, thanks to the Snapdragon X chip inside. The 16 GB of RAM is still the main selling point here—if it was any less, I would recommend the XPS 13 in nearly every scenario (but it’s not on sale right now). It’s only real downfall is the touchpad. It feels frustratingly clumsy to use, making precise movements difficult.

#42728. Breaking: Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1560 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Welcome to the Repair Café, Where Neighbors Fight Throwaway Culture

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk.
  • That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus remarked, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”.

Industry observers note that this is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies that sell everything from hiking boots to smartphones and hot water boilers and that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throwaway economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés to be more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

Recent findings suggest that at the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus mentioned. “We are a substantial family.”.

According to recent reports, pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair and decided to give it a second chance.

It has been revealed that “When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”.

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma noted. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”.

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft—according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

In 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Newly introduced York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

Industry observers note that “ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she mentioned. “I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”.

According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

According to recent reports, on a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh-Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reason, and more so they could keep using them.

In a recent development, gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that had stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

Industry observers note that pines recently graduated but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.”.

In a recent development, one of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying new stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.

Industry observers note that when a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the air fryer, they promptly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

Sources indicate that “ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really vital to me and something that I try to do as well,” Pines remarked. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”.

Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, stated he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends,” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”.

Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

“The beauty of it,” Pettus noted, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that—I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not—but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”.

Nish Khandwala and David Eng are building the AI agent platform to serve every function across the health system: clinical, operational, and administrative.

Nish Khandwala and David Eng are building the AI agent platform to serve every function across the health system: clinical, operational, and administrative.

Healthcare hasnât historically been known as a fast or early technology adopter. Researchers struggle to access external data, collaborate with research institutions, and navigate complex regulations. Hospitals and health systems try to create their own tools or implement narrow point solutions from vendors, but they too often stall in experimentation and never reach patient care.

Health systems need the right platform to swiftly adopt AI, so they can refocus their time back on improving patient outcomes and providing better care.

In a recent development, bunkerhill Health is that platform. Their core product, Carebricks, lets health systems create and deploy AI agents across any clinical or operational use case â turning the data a hospital already generates into timely action for the patients who need it. We first backed Nish Khandwala and David Eng at the seed, and we are proud to continue to double down.

Nish did not read about this problem; he lived it. As a graduate student at Stanford, he helped build an algorithm that could estimate a patientâs coronary artery calcium score from a routine chest scan â a signal of cardiovascular risk that normally requires a dedicated, more invasive test. The algorithm was good enough to be published in Nature Digital Medicine. And then it went nowhere. Around the same time, Nishâs father suffered a heart attack, and his CT scan carried the very calcium signals the Stanford algorithm was built to catch. It is one thing to know that proven science sits unused in academic papers. It is another to watch it fail to reach your own family.

In a recent development, that experience taught Nish something non-obvious: the bottleneck in healthcare AI is not the technology, it is everything around it. So Bunkerhill initially built a system that gets an idea from research to the bedside â sourcing data from a consortium of leading academic medical centers, validating the model, shepherding it through FDA clearance, and installing it into the hospital where a clinician and a patient can actually use it. But they ran into another problem: health systems do not have the time or resources to deploy one-off AI solutions. So Bunkerhill built Carebricks to allow any health system to bring their ideas to life with AI agents across clinical, operational, and administrative work in one central platform. Health systems bring the ideas and the clinical judgment, and Bunkerhill turns them into agents.

We have watched this compound in the field. At UTMB Health, Bunkerhill rapidly went from one agent in production to more than twenty, spreading from one specialty to the next as clinicians saw what it could do. And just as importantly, it has allowed UTMB to consolidate what used to be multiple vendorsâ point solutions into a single platform with Carebricks.

Bunkerhillâs agents run quietly in the background, surfacing the findings that matter and catching the cases the system would have missed. Not to automate clinicians away, but to automate manually-intensive work so clinicians and their teams can focus more time on what they do best: caring for their patients.

Industry observers note that nish and David are outlier founders with the technical depth and the relentlessness this problem demands, and they are pulling healthcare toward faster iteration and better outcomes for every patient, not just the average one. We are excited to partner with Nish, David, and the entire Bunkerhill team as they build the agentic AI platform for healthcare.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is a great time to buy a new pair of headphones. Brands have largely finished launching their latest models for the year, and I'm seeing some stellar Black Friday headphone deals on new and older headphones alike. I've been reviewing headphones (and covering Black Friday deals) for more than four years, so I have a good handle on what's worth opening your wallet for. (Spoilers: it's Sony and Bose this year).

All the deals below are WIRED-tested products we stand by, including wireless earbuds and over-ear headphones. For more Black Friday deals, check out our guides to the Best Black Friday TV Deals and the Best Black Friday Mattress Deals.

Sources indicate that apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds not only for anyone with an iPhone—but also for anyone who wants to keep things simple. They sound great and have some of the best active-noise-canceling (ANC) and transparency modes on the market. They also seamlessly sync with all of your Apple devices. At $100 off, it's the lowest price they've ever been at.

Industry observers note that this is the lowest price I’ve ever seen on one of my favorite pairs of wireless earbuds. The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro have one magic trick: call quality. To put it simply, I sound better talking on calls using these earbuds than any other I’ve tested, and it’s not a close competition. Beyond that, they’re solid all-rounders, with good noise-canceling, sound quality, and versatility.

In a recent development, want workout earbuds that won't fall out? Get these Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. They're some of the more secure-fitting earbuds I've ever tested. Plus, they have great noise-canceling, transparency, and even built-in heart-rate sensors, so you can track your workout even if you left your fitness tracker at home.

The Nothing Ear (3a) are one of our favorite pairs of earbuds under $100, and 30 percent off is the biggest discount I've ever seen for them so far. They have a semi-transparent design and bold colors that stand out from the crowd (particularly the yellow version). While the automated noise-canceling isn't the best, it's hard to fault them at this upcoming low price.

Sources indicate that my main gripe with the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) is price. At 45 percent off (their lowest price ever), that complaint vanishes, making this a top headphone deal to shop. The headphones are exceedingly comfortable and have excellent ANC—far better than basically every other set of headphones at this new low price of $200.

Recent findings suggest that did you hear the news? Sony made a version two of their cult-classic Sony WH-1000XM4 headphones. This is the first time they are on sale, and at $200, are one of the best deals this Black Friday. They have outstanding sound, great noise-canceling, a comfortable fit, and a convenient, folding design well-suited for travel.

Recent findings suggest that the Nothing Headphone (1) are a home run in looks and sound, and they are at their lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday. They’re solid noise cancelers with a bold, transparent design on the ear cups that's somehow techy, retro, and futuristic-looking. Among their best features are the on-ear controls, namely the clicky wheel that adjusts volume and the flat rocker paddle that you can push back and forth to move to the previous track or skip ahead, respectively.

The budget Nothing Headphone (a) and premium Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are also on sale, but the Headphone (1) is the most appealing deal in my view.

The more premium XM6 and the newly revived (and cheaper) XM4C have effectively replaced the Sony WH-1000XM5. But I am still seeing the blue colorway of these excellent headphones at the lowest price I've clocked for these older cans. When they introduced in 2022, they were our top pick for over-ear headphones. They remain excellent and far outperform other options at this limited price.

Sony recently rolled out the WH-CN730N to replace these headphones, hence the rock-bottom price of 50 percent off. While these headphones can't compete with most specs of more premium options on this list, they're ultra-lightweight at just 192 grams. That weight plus 35 hours of battery life with ANC on is nothing to scoff at.

Industry observers note that airPods Max 2 are excellent over-ear headphones for Apple fans, but the $550 sticker price is frankly absurd. Thankfully, they are almost always a little bit on sale, including now. This is far from the best deal I've seen on these headphones, and I do expect the price to dip further during Black Friday sales events, so I would add them to my cart and wait to pull the trigger.

My top over-ear headphone pick, the best-in-class Sony WH-1000XM6, is at its lowest price ever this Black Friday. These headphones are amazing across the board, with their high comfort, superior sound quality, and great noise-canceling capability.

Partnering with Etched: Building the Inference Machine

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.
  • Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.
  • Inference is on the path to becoming the largest market in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.

Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.

Inference is on the path to becoming the largest market in the world.

If this AI dream is everything we hope it to be â and so far, the signs point to ever-increasing acceleration of capabilities â then inference will power every storefront, every movie, every medical encounter, every video game, every lawsuit, every line of code.

Industry observers note that today, the inference market is so obviously large that building an inference-specific system is consensus. Back in 2022, when Gavin, Chris, and Rob were still in their dorm rooms at Harvard, that bet was deeply contrarian. The result: Etched is the only post-ChatGPT-era hardware startup with production-ready custom silicon, ready to ship in 2026.

Over the past years, Etched has pioneered several research breakthroughs â low voltage inference and cluster-scale memory â each a hard-won architectural choice that drives step-change gains in throughput and latency. As the unit of compute has moved from the chip to the rack to the cluster, Etched has designed for that reality, building not just chips, but cluster-scale inference systems. Driven by these fundamental innovations, Etchedâs inference system excels in throughput and interactivity on the full span of frontier models â from large sparse MoEs, to dense transformers, to alternative architectures entirely, like Mamba.

Believing this is one thing. Building it is another entirely. Novel computing hardware is among the hardest things in the world to get right, and the ground underneath is constantly moving. Models change every few weeks, context lengths stretch, attention gets reinvented, the mix of dense and sparse keeps shifting. Winning here means doing two things simultaneously: iterating fast enough to keep pace with the models, and pushing the frontier of what the hardware can do. That takes a rare kind of team: visionary enough to create the right designs, young enough to move fast, proven enough to have chips in production, and built to do this for decades, not a single tape-out.

Industry observers note that walking into the Etched office for the first time is like a bolt of lightning. Go in the morning or at 11 p.m. â the energy is the same, and it is infectious. Gavin and Rob are the kind of outliers both daring enough to design silicon from first principles and bold enough to knock down every obstacle in their path, and the team they have assembled matches them. We have watched them do the things that separate those who merely talk about hardware from those who ship it: standing up a live lab in San Jose to host their first racks; opening an office in Taiwan to colocate with suppliers and expedite testing; questioning every single assumption for what is possible, such as low voltage inference. âProduction is the productâ is the companyâs mantra. Shipping is all that matters.

It has been revealed that the companyâs progress has been rapid. Earlier this year, Etched taped out its first generation chip at TSMC, making it the first post-ChatGPT-era company with a successful full-reticle A0 chip tape-out on TSMCâs leading-edge nodes. Then, in a span of just 40 days, the Etched team brought up their first cluster of chips to run inference on a wide range of frontier AI models, achieving Pareto dominant performance on industry-standard throughput-interactivity curves. Now, Etchedâs earliest customers are getting access to the product, seeing for themselves the speed, throughput, and expressiveness of the system.

Etched has built a beautiful machine in Gen 1. We expect it will do very well in the market. But we are partnering with Etched because we believe they have built the rarest thing in this industry: the machine that builds the machine. This is a team that has the taste and the relentless execution to keep shipping the next generation of inference machines, faster and more ambitious each time.

Recent findings suggest that the intelligence race is fundamentally compute constrained. Pushing the limits of physics to deliver the maximum intelligence per watt is both an insanely fun engineering and operations problem, and an incredibly noble mission for humanity.

We are delighted to be partnering with Etched and leading their $300 Million Series C at a $10 Billion pre-money valuation, joined by our friends at Jane Street, Andreessen Horowitz, Diffusion, and SK Hynix.

I’m often asked if Dyson products are really worth the money. As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum—from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones you should buy and at what price. The best time to shop is during sale season, and lucky for you, Dyson Black Friday deals have arrived for you to scoop up a new stick vacuum or even a handy robot vacuum.

If a new vacuum is on your wishlist this holiday season, or a loved one's (my dad is obsessed with the Dyson), then Black Friday is your best shot at a great deal ahead of the holiday season. Here's the best sales happening on Dyson vacuums I've tested and love.

Updated November 27, 2027: This story has been updated for Black Friday with more deals, and we checked that prices are still accurate.

If you want a cheaper vacuum that still comes with two cleaner heads, the older Dyson V15 Detect is also already on sale ($599), and it's even bundled with the Car Cleaning Kit, meaning three extra attachments. The V15 was our top Dyson vacuum pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still packs two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). America’s Open-Model Paradox

📅 24 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China increasingly supplies the models Western companies use to serve, train, and build AI.
  • According to recent reports, qwenâs share of upcoming open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOMâs Report.
  • Industry observers note that this dependence now extends upstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China increasingly supplies the models Western companies use to serve, train, and build AI.

According to recent reports, qwenâs share of upcoming open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOMâs Report. The majority of American AI startups seem to be using Chinese open weights somewhere in their stack.

Industry observers note that this dependence now extends upstream. Western application companies are building on Chinese Open Source models. Further, Western labs are using Chinese models as teachers and sources of synthetic training data in the torrid race to close the frontier gap.

For example, Thinking Machines pre-trained Inkling independently, but used synthetic data generated by Moonshotâs Kimi K2.5 to bootstrap its supervised fine-tuning.

The relevant point is not how much of Inkling came from Kimi. The point is that a Western lab had a legal path to learn from a Chinese open model, while equivalent use of GPT or Claude outputs is prohibited.

The flow today looks something like this:.

Western frontier models â alleged unauthorized foreign extraction â Chinese open weights â lawful Western post-training.

American frontier models â lawful Western post-training.

Why does that matter? Pre-training creates a capable base model. Post-training turns it into a useful coding, reasoning, tool-using, and agentic system. A stronger teacher converts part of that expensive discovery process into a cheaper learning problem.

In a recent development, distillation does not explain Chinaâs entire open-model lead. Chinese labs have world-class researchers, substantial compute, strong pre-trained models, software-hardware codesign, and rapidly improving post-training capabilities. But distillation compresses the costly final gap between a strong base and a near-frontier system. Even if distillation represents a smaller share of  a Chinese modelâs total capability, it represents a meaningful share of its advantage over American open models.

Sources indicate that newly introduced enforcement mechanisms will make large-scale distillation harder, slower, and more expensive for Chinese companies. However, enforcement will not eliminate distillation baked by state actors. Every Western frontier advance therefore creates another teacher for Chinese labs. Western builders must either reproduce those capabilities independently or wait to learn from Chinese models.

This gap gives Chinese labs a recurring structural advantage over Western companies.

It has been revealed that the stakes extend far beyond model revenue. Suppliers of the open layer become the default base for products, synthetic data, post-training systems, evals, agents, optimization, and applied AI.

The prize is to become the substrate on which global enterprises build and improve digital intelligence.The Weights Are Open. Our Dependency Is Not.

Sources indicate that downloading a Chinese model gives a Western firm control over the particular version. It can run the model locally, modify it, and continue using it without permission.

In a recent development, but AI capability is an upgrade cycle. Western startups, model developers, and researchers increasingly rely on each fresh Qwen, Kimi, GLM, or DeepSeek as a stronger base, a teacher, a source of synthetic data, and a platform for further research.

In a recent development, if China stops releasing its strongest models, existing products will not break. They will fall behind. Reuters recently reported that Chinese authorities have discussed restricting overseas access to advanced models, including models that have not yet been released. No final policy has been declared, but Western access ultimately depends on Chinese labs and regulators continuing to publish.

There is also a more technical security problem. An open-weight model is not necessarily an auditable model.

In a recent development, the weights are the compressed result of training. They do not reveal the full pre-training corpus, which data was filtered or poisoned, what interventions were made during training, or whether rare trigger-dependent behavior was embedded.

We are not alleging that Qwen, Kimi, or another Chinese model contains a backdoor. The point is that possessing the weights cannot prove the absence of one. A backdoor can remain dormant during ordinary testing and activate only when an unknown trigger appears. Research shows that deliberately implanted behavior can survive supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training.

According to recent reports, that may be an acceptable supply-chain risk for many consumer applications. It is not acceptable for defense, intelligence, or critical infrastructure.

It has been revealed that open weights provide control over deployment. They do not guarantee continued access to better models, nor alignment, trust and safety in the model itself.

A Framework For A Direct American Path.

American companies need a legal way to turn American frontier capability into cheaper, ownable models.

Without a domestic route, the West may lead at the closed frontier while falling into dependence on China for the open layer.

A useful framework has three parts.

According to recent reports, keep building Western base models: Reflection (building open super-intelligence for enterprises & sovereigns), TML, and Nemotron are making incredible progress. But stronger pre-training alone does not solve the teacher problem. American builders also need a lawful way to absorb capabilities already developed at the American frontier.

It has been revealed that create controlled teacher access: Frontier labs could sell structured training rights to qualifying Western and allied companies, whether the resulting models are released openly or deployed privately. Access could trail the frontier, cover defined capabilities, be limited to verified companies, and be metered and audited. The most sensitive biological and cyber capabilities could remain restricted. This would not allow companies to clone the newest frontier model. It would create a legal, priced route for capability transfer that sophisticated foreign actors are already pursuing covertly.

Keep raising the cost of foreign distillation: Better identity verification, access controls, proxy disruption, and enforcement should continue. If a voluntary market does not develop, access could eventually become a condition attached to major federal AI contracts, for example.

These are starting points. Who qualifies, how far access should trail the frontier, how it should be priced, and which capabilities remain restricted are topics that deserve real debate.

Imagine if we had not allowed for training on the open web. We would have no leading AI at all. These types of policy implications are transformative. All the leading labs benefited from copious amounts of openly available data. We have to have an open and free future: It is imperative for Western competitiveness.

What should no longer go unquestioned is the current equilibrium: the West creates the frontier, part of that capability travels indirectly through Chinese models, and Western builders then depend on those models to make intelligence cheaper, adaptable, and sovereign.

To distill or not to distill is not the question. The question is whether the West creates a legal domestic path for capability transfer â or  relies  on an indirect path through China.

What’s So Great About Merino Wool?

Sources indicate that merino wool is great because you're stealing a sheep's ability to keep itself warm or cool based on the temperatures it's in. This is a process often referred to as thermoregulation. Merino sheep have thinner, softer wool than what most people think of when they think of wool. The sheep evolved this soft coat to keep them comfortable across a wide range of temperatures. The result is a fabric that's comfortable to wear next to your skin. For the softest tees, look for fabrics that are either superfine or ultrafine—anything 17 µm or higher—like Unbound's T-shirts.

Industry observers note that wool is sustainable, too. One sheep can produce 4 to 5 pounds of wool per year. While cotton has its place, and so does the occasional synthetic garment, merino wool is a remarkable fabric that's the cornerstone of my wardrobe. I don't think you can have too many merino pieces in your closet, but they’re not cheap, which is why we're featuring these deals.

What’s So Great About Unbound Merino?

I like Unbound's T-shirts because they're 100 percent merino wool, no synthetics involved. That means all the antibacterial, odor-resistant, moisture-wicking, temperature-regulating goodness of merino wool … just works. I've found Unbound's T-shirts in particular to be very quick-drying and wrinkle resistant, two of the reasons I think they're the best merino T-shirts for travel. The tech giant's pants also have a very high wool percentage (95 percent), and they roll up nicely, making them very packable. Do you need special travel clothing? No, but Unbound's merino wool is naturally odor-resistant, which means you need fewer pieces in your bag. The company also offers a 30-day guarantee. If you don't like it, you can send it back.

According to recent reports, most merino products come with care instructions. Unbound Merino's T-shirts should be washed cold with like colors, then laid flat to dry. Whatever you do, don't bleach them and don't tumble dry them. The latter is especially destructive. I do it to every wool T-shirt I test, and it makes me sad, but I know some of you won't listen and will do it anyway, so I have to know what happens so I can warn you. Don't tumble dry. Just put it on a drying rack. It doesn't take more than a day. Seriously, you just spent $80 (on sale!) on a T-shirt; take care of it. Properly cared for, high-quality merino clothing like Unbound's is incredibly durable and will last for years. Throw it in the dryer and the pilling starts almost immediately.

Do I always lay them flat to dry? No. When traveling I usually hand-wash in the sink and then drape them over the shower curtain rod to dry, which hasn't seemed to have much negative impact. The complications with hanging wool to dry is that it will stretch out from the water weight. This is particularly true with 100 percent merino, like Unbound's T-shirts.

I've never had a problem storing merino in my closet between wears, but for long-term storage, I recommend you take precautions against moths, which are notorious for eating holes in wool. I have lost merino garments to moths. I make sure to wash and thoroughly dry whatever I am storing, then I seal it in a compression bag. Another option is to put your merino garment in a cotton bag or otherwise wrap it in cotton and then put it in a plastic bin. It's very key to make sure that the garment is completely dry before using any of these storage methods; otherwise your wool will smell musty and moldy. Other options include storing your garment in a cedar chest, which is a good natural deterrent for moths, or use moth traps or lavender sachets, which will repel the moths.

Unbound Merino (Unbound Merino Women’s).

The final thing I love about these is how fast they dry. In most climates, you can give it a wash in the sink at night, roll it up in a towel, wring it dry, lay it out flat, and it'll be dry by morning. If they have a downside, it's that Unbound's T-shirts do need to be babied a little. To help them last a long time I recommend hand washing and line-drying. Danny, Amit, Yotam, Tamar, Yonatan and their teams are joining forces to build a complete security platform for the age of AI.

According to recent reports, in 2021, before Oasis Security was even founded, I sat down with co-founder Danny Brickman and came away thinking he had something familiar. He showed the same drive weâd seen in the founders of two other Sequoia companies, Wiz and Cyera, whose founders, like Danny, had come up through Talpiot, the leadership program of the IDF. I wrote about that meeting a couple of years later in my investment memo, when we backed Oasis Security, at the Series A. I didnât realize at the time how literally connected that comparison would turn out to be. Today, Oasis is joining Cyera â and it turns out the foundersâ stories make the case for this combination almost as well as the technology does.

In a recent development, three years ago, the pitch for Oasis was simple: enterprises were about to have far more machine identities than human ones, and almost nobody had a real way to manage or secure them. That was true then. Itâs far more true now. Every AI agent creates or uses non-human identities â API keys, service accounts, OAuth tokens, agent-to-agent credentials â that act with real permissions and real blast radius, and that donât behave anything like the human identities the last generation of identity tooling was built around. AI drove non-human identity from a niche IAM subcategory to a board-level CISO conversation. Danny Brickman and his co-founder Amit Zimerman built Oasis, which they call agentic access management, for exactly that world.

According to recent reports, cyera arrived at the same shift from a different direction. Yotam Segev, Tamar Bar-Ilan, and Yonatan Itai built the company to answer a deceptively simple question: where does an organizationâs sensitive data actually live, who can reach it, and whatâs really at risk? As AI agents started reading, writing and acting on that data, they reached a conclusion that now looks obvious: securing AI means securing the data, the identities acting on it (human and non-human), and the agents themselves.

Sources indicate that put the two products side by side, and they complement each other perfectly. Cyera knows where the sensitive data is. Oasis knows who or what can actually touch it â every service account, API key and agent credential, and whether itâs behaving the way it should. Itâs a bit like a bank vault: the best way to protect it is by knowing both whatâs inside and whoâs approaching. Data security tells you whatâs actually at stake. Identity security tells you whether the thing touching your data is legitimate. Together, the two products cover the entire path an AI agent takes through a companyâs environment, from the data it touches to the identity it uses to touch it.

Sources indicate that thereâs a practical case here too. Cyera has built one of the most powerful enterprise GTM teams, with the kind of scale that usually takes a startup a decade to reach. Oasisâs product now gets to run through that engine, into enterprise accounts it would otherwise have taken years to earn on its own. And the market isnât waiting: Whoever builds the first genuinely complete AI security platform, spanning data, identity and agents, has a real shot at becoming the default layer enterprises standardize on as agentic AI rolls out. Speed and completeness both matter, and the combination of Cyera and Oasis creates both.

The foundersâ backgrounds make the fit feel almost inevitable in hindsight. Itâs a small world: two teams weâd backed independently, drawn from the same pool of Israeli technical talent, ended up building the two halves of the same answer to AI security. Talpiot and Unit 8200 alumni have produced a disproportionate share of the last decadeâs significant cybersecurity companies, so the coincidence is smaller than it looks, but itâs still a good sign when it plays out this cleanly.

Industry observers note that danny, Amit and the Oasis team built the category-defining tech giant in non-human identity in under three years, from a standing start to a product enterprises trust with agentic access at scale. That doesnât happen without genuinely hard technical work, and a founder team that saw the shift to agentic AI before almost anyone else in security did. We at Sequoia have backed both Cyera and Oasis since their Series A rounds, and weâre proud to keep backing this team as they take on the next chapter together â a bigger stage, and an opportunity sized to match.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Cybersecurity is a perpetual fight between the good guys and the bad. The age of agentic AI and Mythos-class models has tipped the scales in favor of the bad guys, opening a Pandoraâs box for offensive capabilities. An explosion in CVEs has since ensued.

Cyberattacks are about technical exploitation, which requires coding and reasoning prowess. Anthropicâs Mythos can discover and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities. Any model paired with a harness brings the cost of social engineering attacks down to near zero, unleashing them at unprecedented scale. The danger is heightened with every upcoming model release.

Defensive security isnât improving in parallel. The relevant data lives in logs, events, traces and telemetry, a fundamentally different modality than the bodies of text LLMs usually train on, which barely show up in pretraining. Unlike offensive cybersecurity, which involves goal-directed reasoning towards a defined objective, defense requires open-ended reasoning, continually finding anomalies across vast amounts of normal-looking activity, a distinct capability that typically demands extensive domain-specific training. In short, defense is out of distribution for general-purpose frontier models: neither the data nor the intuition it requires is well-represented in training. In the race toward AGI, we cannot expect the frontier labs to take the detour of overhauling their training pipelines for defensive cybersecurity. And we certainly canât afford to bet our security on a hope that they do.

Corma has illustrated this âdefense gapâ in testing. They ran red/blue team simulations where an attacker plants a hidden backdoor and a defender tries to find it. The defender failed to find the backdoor 78% of the time, even when the defender was an identical copy of the very same model that planted it. Holding model quality constant, attackers will always have an advantage.

Recent findings suggest that the only answer to scaling laws on offense is better scaling laws on defense. Recent events have shown that frontier AI for defensive cybersecurity is one of the crucial unsolved problems of the AI age. Solving it is the generational mission Corma was founded on.

Corma founder and CEO Alon Pluda and his team are training a foundation model to power defensive cybersecurity agents. Cybersecurity, like Go or chess, is a two-player, zero-sum game with a clean reward (were you breached or not?) and an endless supply of games to play. Reinforcement learning and self-play have produced superhuman results before in this kind of paradigm. We are seeing history repeat itself. Corma pushes this further with large-scale reinforcement learning across cybersecurity environments that replicate real enterprise networks, with all their tools, telemetry and noise â as part of a training pipeline that produces frontier defensive capabilities, outperforming general-purpose foundation models, with much lower per-token inference costs.

It has been revealed that in the cat-and-mouse game of cybersecurity, we believe Cormaâs vertical integration and âsovereign AIâ approach will win. Cost matters (always-on inference costs can rack up swiftly). Owning the model weights matters (they arenât subject to restrictions on cybersecurity-related usage set by the closed model labs). And specialization and inference speed really matter (fastest to protect against a newly introduced threat wins).

Industry observers note that cormaâs foundation model is deployed and productized as an agentic Security Workforce. These workers operate across different security tools and take on roles spanning the entire security organization: from security operations and identity management to cloud and network security and beyond. They are on the job at Fortune 500 companies and large enterprises across healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, retail and more.

Sources indicate that cormaâs foundation model powers agents that complete defensive work end to end. We spoke to one CISO whose Corma agent notified him of a pending attack through his Garmin watch while he was on a walk with his dog in the evening; with one confirmation, the agent was able to shut the attacker down, all while he was still walking. In another instance, within its first hour on the job, Corma uncovered, contained and remediated an active attacker campaign inside a customerâs network that their security team had missed for 52 days.

Training frontier foundation models for defensive cybersecurity requires world-class hackers and world-class researchers â almost no firm on earth has both. Alon is personally one of the most elite hackers in the world, and has assembled a cohesive and interdisciplinary team of hackers and researchers that is hill-climbing on technical challenges and building impressive commercial momentum.

We are thrilled to lead Cormaâs seed round and to be their partner as they chart newly introduced territory in what is sure to be one of the most dynamic races in AI.

Stefan and Veljko are building the AI-native workspace for quality video creation.

Stefan and Veljko are building the AI-native workspace for quality video creation.

Thereâs something magical about watching a developer in flow state, fingers flying as they type into Codex, Claude, or Cursor. A powerful creation interface unfolds in response to every keystroke, powering a workflow that would have been unrecognizable, even alien-like, to any professional software engineer just two years ago. The entire IDE has been torn down and rebuilt from scratch for the age of AI, and developers are flying as a result.

Video models have raced ahead over the same two years. Yet unlike coding, video creation remains stuck in the stone age, with its entire toolchain still built around capturing, uploading, storing, and editing enormous files.

Generative video is at a threshold moment: the models are now expressive enough to become the new camera. The bottleneck is no longer the technical art of animation or the $100M budgets for film crews and visual effects; itâs human creativity and token inference. But video creators are not yet flying.

Without a proper AI-native tool suite, or a âCursor for video,â the people who make films, TV series, and commercials for a living remain stuck bolting model outputs onto legacy editing pipelines. Generation, review, and production tracking each live in a separate application; workflows buckle under the sheer volume of material; and a finished take often canât be traced back to its source for legal clearance. Itâs a gaping problem and is the biggest roadblock on the industryâs path to truly embracing AI.

Preview clears that block. An AI-native video creation and production platform built for professional creators, Preview combines a video timeline with an infinite canvas for ideation into one collaborative multiplayer workspace. Teams can generate with any model and track every character, location, and prop, with complete records of how every asset was made. It enables both halves of a hybrid production to work together seamlessly. There is simply nothing like it in the market.

Recent findings suggest that co-founders Stefan Fejes and Veljko Tornjanski have been best friends since high school in Serbia, and were seemingly born for this mission. They were founding team members at video creation pioneer Veed; later, at Vizcom, Veljko was the first hire and became Head of AI, while Stefan led Product. They understand well the tricky nuances of video, they have deep empathy for their customers, and they have delivered sophisticated, polished work on impressively short timelines.

According to recent reports, more than 100 studios are already actively using Preview, from agencies making commercials for Fortune 500 brands to AI-native studios to Hollywood feature filmmakers. Simply put, they love it. Customers tell us it has become the most significant tool in their work, and the single source of truth from which all downstream inference flows.

We are at the precipice of a video token tsunami, and many billions of dollars of inference will run through this category, driving the next wave of iconic films and IP. Value will accrue to where the work actually happensâthe platform a creative team opens in the morning and closes at night, where the decisions get made and the record gets kept. We believe Preview is that platform, and that this is the right team, the right product, and the right moment. We are thrilled to partner with Stefan and Veljko and to lead their seed round.

Recent findings suggest that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

In a recent development, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.

Recently, Alex Karp encouraged enterprises to âown the means of production.â Not long after, Satya Nadella declared that buying intelligence from a frontier lab is like paying twice: once with money, and once with the proprietary knowledge you reveal to make that intelligence useful.

The question everyone is asking: who should own the intelligence at the core of your business?

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, owning your intelligence is not a mandate nor a recommendation to get off the labs. For many workloads, frontier APIs and agents are still the right answer. But across our portfolio, we are seeing more companies building their own AI capabilities for parts of their products, vertically integrating toward owning and shaping their weights.

A few weeks ago, Sequoia brought together a group of AI founders and builders for an event on owning your AI stack. We had Harvey give us the customer-back view. Then Mercor, Langchain, Trajectory, and Fireworks walked us through the technical building blocks in the post-training stack.

Across the talks, a clear playbook emerged.

First, the open-weight frontier has moved faster than anticipated. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are extremely good! Training on open models used to be a treadmillâ¦ you mightâve spent months fine-tuning, and the next frontier release would erase your gains. Now, you can start from a baseline close to the frontier.

Second, the independent post-training stack has matured. Thanks to companies like Mercor and Fireworks, every company can access the technology stack of a frontier research lab, from training to inference to human or synthetic data. With strong evals, harness engineering, post-training, and online learning, open models can now beat frontier models in specific domains.

Sources indicate that A year ago, you chose open weights when performance was something you could sacrifice. Now, it is becoming an existential and strategic question. The newest battleground is for the intelligence layer. Not your weights, not your product.

Thereâs no one-size-fits-all approach. In addition to performance, there may be slices of your product where renting intelligence becomes a constraint because ofâ¦.

1. Cost. The more successful your AI product, the higher your AI COGS. If inference costs scale directly with usage, owning the model is the best way to protect your margins.

Sources indicate that 2. Speed. If youâre operating in a domain like coding (tab autocomplete) or cybersecurity, a small distilled custom model might beat a large general one, because speed is so important.

3. Proprietary data. If your feedback, evals, customer interactions, or domain data are what make the system better, you might prefer that data stays within your walls.

According to recent reports, 4. Controlling your destiny. The app layer and the intelligence layer are starting to merge. The labs are moving up into product, and app companies are moving down into the training loops that define how the product thinks. Owning the product increasingly might mean controlling more of the learning loop and the intelligence itself (h/t Harvey Research, RampLabs, Glean, Factory, and more).

It has been revealed that assuming you've decided on your strategy for what to own vs. rent, the question becomes: how do you go from zero to one?

Build your team. Don't shoehorn this into a platform team. Owning your intelligence needs people playing offense: building evals, shaping data, experimenting with open models, tuning harnesses, and pushing performance in a domain. Small, de novo teams go very far here, partnering with half a dozen ecosystem partners. Harvey, for example, has done a surprising amount of research with a team of just seven people!

In a recent development, make the work legible. Every buyer right now is choosing their AI champion. Increasingly, the tiebreaker is published research, benchmarks, or technical posts. If you choose to do wonderful research in-house, share it with the ecosystem.

Sources indicate that execute the technical steps. Weâve laid out a high level framework below.

Harveyâs Gabe Pereyra mentioned it well: "If you don't have a good benchmark, you can't train models.â.

In a recent development, an eval is a set of tasks that measures whether your system can do the work well. Every task contains a prompt, context the model can use, and a grader. Most evals start as a founder squinting at outputs and vibe-checking whether they feel right. The goal is to turn that judgement into something repeatable.

In a recent development, harvey built its Legal Agent Benchmark by turning real legal work into discrete tasks a model could be tested on. The first iteration includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

Itâs important to have an eval before making the decision to own your intelligence. Once every forward pass has an eval, deciding which model to use can be a measured decision instead of a guess.

2/ Harness and context engineering.

An agent has three parts: the model, the context, and the harness. The harness governs the product logic around the model: routing, retrieval, tools, memory, fallbacks, and traces. Harrison Chaseâs simple framing was that "the main job of the harness is to bring context to the model at the right point in time." The more out of distribution the task is for the model, the worse the off-the-shelf harness will be.

A good harness lets you route tasks to the best model for your specific job, reuse the same evals across models, and decide what context and tools an agent gets. It also makes the agent inspectable. You can trace what context went in, which tools were called, and where it got stuck.

It has been revealed that post-training covers several techniques. The right one depends on what youâre trying to improve.

Industry observers note that lin Qiao laid it out: if the model is missing facts, you don't need to post-train - just use context or RAG. If the output format or behavior is wrong, use supervised fine-tuning. If the glitch is product taste, use preference tuning. If the model needs to improve at a specialized task, use RL. If the model is too slow or expensive, distill it.

The goal is to pick the lightest method that moves your eval. Then serve the model through the same harness and measure quality, latency, and cost as it runs.

Once the system has its pieces â evals, harness, and model â the final step is improving that system in production.

Sources indicate that arjun Karanam made a good point: models keep getting smarter, but every session feels like it's their first day on the job. You can put Terence Tao in an accounting firm, but chances are (at least on day 1) he wonât be the best accountant there. What's missing is experience, not intelligence. Agents create that experience as they run.

Sources indicate that A trajectory is the path through the task: the context the model saw, the tools and sub-agents it called, the answer it produced, and what the user edited, undid, or retried. Capturing those trajectories in a tool like LangChain's LangSmith is necessary to build a continuous production loop. A failed task becomes an eval. Missing information goes into context or memory. A bad tool response becomes a harness fix.

Buyer beware: owning your intelligence opens Pandoraâs box.

Industry observers note that the closed-model stack is simple. You call a frontier model, use an out-of-the-box harness (e.g., Claude Code or Codex), add prompts and context, and ship. That gives you a high floor, but also a lower ceiling.

In a recent development, owning your stack means taking on more of the system yourself. The production stack becomes your open-source model, custom harness, tools, and context. The development stack becomes your proprietary evals, domain data, and online learning loop.

It is certainly more work! It potentially gives you a lower floor â but it also raises the ceiling.

The labs will keep building the giant brains. We should all use them.

It has been revealed that but, in parallel, the best product companies are growing their own little geniuses: fast, opinionated, domain-obsessed, and tuned to the work they see. In a world where more companies take ownership of their own intelligence, the ecosystem flourishes and individuality triumphs.

Thatâs the promise of a world where companies own their intelligence. And weâre delighted to see the progress from the little guys, the startups that want to bring that world into existence.

I first met Mateo Jaramillo, the CEO of Form Energy, in spring 2020. It was a memorable meeting because it was the first in-person founder meeting I had in the COVID pandemic and we were all wearing masks. At that time, Mateo described a simple idea: solar and wind were going to take over the grid, but we needed batteries to store that energy. Lithium-ion was a great chemistry for cars, and it could store grid-scale energy for 4-6 hours, but it was never going to store energy for multiple days. Thinking from first principles, Mateo, who previously started and ran Teslaâs energy business, had assembled the battery Avengers, including legendary battery scientist Yet-Ming Chiang as Chief Scientist and Billy Woodford as CTO. The team set their sights on building an iron-air battery: iron, because itâs cheap and abundant, and air, because itâs free. The goal was to turn those cheap materials into a battery that could compete with gas peaker plants on cost while delivering a clean and reliable baseload energy resource.

According to recent reports, knowing very little about batteries at the time, I reached out to a group of professors to diligence whether the science worked. I ended up selecting a Harvard professor and hired him as a consultant. At the end of the project, he gave us a thumbs up, and as a sign of his excitement, asked if he could roll his consulting fee into our investment.

Recent findings suggest that when I arrived at Sequoia in mid-2023, Mateo was one of my first calls. At that time he was just starting construction on Form Energyâs first high-volume battery manufacturing facility, located on a shuttered steel mill site in West Virginia. I flew out for a factory visit with my partner Isaiah Boone in July 2024, and we were astounded. So many companies come to us talking about reindustrializing America, and here was a company that was actually doing it, and creating more than 400 fresh jobs along the way. Given that China is the epicenter of battery manufacturing globally, we were energized by the potential to build a US national battery champion, starting with a fundamentally new technology, which is what America excels at.

Industry observers note that the following year, the manufacturer went through what is colloquially termed âproduction hell.â This is exactly what Tesla, SpaceX and others had gone through before them. If you really want to reindustrialize this country, these things donât happen overnight, and they are far from easy. Companies that go through this gauntlet come out sturdier and stronger. To Mateo and the teamâs credit, they doubled down. He had by then relocated his entire family from San Francisco to Western Pennsylvania, a short drive from the plant. Having experienced this type of scaling at Tesla, Mateo knew what to do: live it, sleep it, breathe it â until you've pulled through.

Recent findings suggest that and pull through he did. I knew heâd turned the corner when finally, the manufacturer received the order that everyone knew would eventually come: a large hyperscale project. Nine years in, Form had done the thing it set out to do: build battery systems that can compete with gas. In the meantime, luck worked in their favor too: AI provided a huge catalyst in the market, where suddenly rebuilding the grid went from ânice to haveâ to âneed to have.â As an AI investor, this company, which had spent years building deep relationships with utilities and regulators, was now in a prime position to serve emergent AI demand.

The opportunity to now scale up from a handful of initial projects toward completely transforming the US grid is tremendous.
